Hiring an Air Duct Cleaner? EPA's Consumer Checklist, Step by Step #Shorts
videos.description:
Thinking about having your air ducts cleaned? EPA's consumer guide includes a checklist for choosing a service provider. Here it is, straight from the guide.

KEY POINTS
• Start with the why: EPA does not recommend that air ducts be cleaned routinely, but only as needed — for example, if ducts are visibly contaminated with substantial mold growth, pests or vermin, or clogged with substantial deposits of dust or debris.
• An honest note: EPA's guide states that duct cleaning has never been shown to actually prevent health problems, and studies don't conclusively show that dust levels in homes increase because of dirty air ducts.
• Get 3 estimates: talk to at least three different service providers and get written estimates before deciding.
• Ask to see it: ask the providers to show you the contamination that would justify cleaning. For apparent mold, EPA suggests lab confirmation or your own judgment.
• Check references: make sure other customers were satisfied, and check with your county or city consumer affairs office or the Better Business Bureau for complaints.
• Ask how they work: confirm they are experienced with systems like yours, use procedures to protect you, your pets and your home, and comply with NADCA's air duct cleaning standards (and NAIMA's recommendations for fiberglass duct board or lined ducts). Don't allow chemical biocides or treatments unless you fully understand the pros and cons. EPA also notes it does not certify or endorse duct cleaning companies.
• Get it in writing: a written agreement outlining the total cost and scope of the job before work begins.
EPA also recommends having fuel-burning furnaces, stoves and fireplaces inspected and serviced before each heating season.

videos.title: Painting Over Mold? 3 Cleanup Mistakes and What EPA Recommends Instead #Shorts
videos.description:
Spotted a small patch of mold at home? Three common cleanup mistakes, and what EPA recommends instead.

KEY POINTS
• Mistake 1 – Painting over it: EPA says do not paint or caulk moldy surfaces; paint applied over moldy surfaces is likely to peel. EPA's disaster cleanup guide adds that painting or caulking over mold will not prevent mold from growing.
• Do this instead: fix the water problem completely, clean up all the mold, and dry the surfaces before you paint or caulk.
• Mistake 2 – Bleach as step one: EPA says using a biocide such as chlorine bleach is not recommended as a routine practice during mold cleanup (professional judgment may call for it in some cases, such as when immune-compromised people are present). Scrub mold off hard surfaces with detergent and water, and dry completely.
• Dead isn't gone: EPA notes dead mold may still cause allergic reactions in some people, so it is not enough to kill mold — it must also be removed.
• Mistake 3 – Saving moldy porous items: absorbent or porous materials such as ceiling tiles and carpet may have to be thrown away if they become moldy, because mold can grow in their empty spaces and crevices.
• If you do use bleach: always ventilate and exhaust the air to the outdoors, and never mix chlorine bleach with cleaners or detergents containing ammonia, because toxic fumes could be produced.
For mold covering more than about 10 square feet, EPA points to its larger remediation guidance and professional help.

videos.description:
Your carbon monoxide alarm starts sounding in the middle of the night. Here's what the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission says to do, step by step.

KEY POINTS
• Step 1 – Don't hunt for it: CPSC says never ignore an alarming CO alarm, and if the alarm signal sounds, do not try to find the source of the CO.
• Step 2 – Get outside now: immediately move outside to fresh air. CPSC's guide for responders advises residents to go outside or to a neighbor's home immediately and not take time to ventilate the home, unless someone is unconscious or cannot leave.
• Step 3 – Call 911: call your emergency services, fire department or 911.
• Step 4 – Head count: after calling 911, do a head count to check that all persons are accounted for.
• Step 5 – Wait for the all-clear: do not re-enter the premises until emergency responders have given you permission.
• Step 6 – Fix before reuse: if a malfunctioning appliance is the source, do not operate it until it has been properly serviced by trained personnel. If your alarm reactivates within 24 hours after returning, repeat the steps and call a qualified appliance technician to check all fuel-burning equipment.
CPSC also lists CO poisoning symptoms — headache, dizziness, weakness, nausea, vomiting, sleepiness and confusion — and says if you suspect CO poisoning, get to fresh air immediately and call 911.

videos.title: Thirdhand Smoke: 3 Myths About the Residue Tobacco Leaves Behind Indoors #Shorts
videos.description:
Thirdhand smoke is the residue tobacco leaves behind indoors. Three common myths, checked against peer-reviewed research.

KEY POINTS
• Myth 1 – Gone when it clears: a peer-reviewed review describes thirdhand smoke as the persistent residue from aged secondhand smoke that adheres to indoor dust and surfaces and re-emits into the air.
• Fact – It changes: Berkeley Lab chemists (Sleiman et al., PNAS 2010) reported that nicotine on surfaces reacts with nitrous acid — an indoor pollutant from sources such as tobacco smoke and unvented or improperly vented gas appliances — to form tobacco-specific nitrosamines, including NNK, which IARC classifies as a human carcinogen.
• Where it shows up: one study found NNK on surfaces in 33 of 37 smokers' homes, but only 3 of 19 nonsmokers' homes.
• Myth 2 – Vaping leaves nothing: Berkeley Lab says aerosolized nicotine released during smoking and vaping adsorbs to indoor surfaces.
• Myth 3 – It's just a smell: a Berkeley Lab analysis (Environmental Science & Technology) estimated that, under typical indoor conditions, NNK doses in thirdhand-smoke-contaminated homes can exceed California's "No Significant Risk Level" guideline.
• Honest limits: thirdhand smoke research is much newer than the roughly 40 years of secondhand smoke research, and the original chemistry papers did not study health effects. Reviewers say the available evidence supports greater efforts to eliminate thirdhand smoke from homes and cars.

SOURCES

videos.title: Lead Dust by the Numbers: What 1978, 5, 40 and 100 Mean in EPA's New Rule #Shorts
videos.description:
EPA's lead dust rules changed recently. Four numbers explain what that means for older homes: 1978, 5, 40 and 100.

KEY POINTS
• 1978: EPA's lead-based paint dust rule applies to pre-1978 homes and childcare facilities.
• Any reportable level: in October 2024, EPA reduced the level of lead in dust considered hazardous — from 10 µg/ft² on floors and 100 µg/ft² on window sills — to any reportable level measured by an EPA-recognized laboratory, recognizing that no safe level of lead in blood has been found for children.
• 5 on floors: the dust-lead action level after an abatement dropped from 10 to 5 micrograms per square foot for floors.
• 40 on window sills: down from 100 µg/ft².
• 100 in window troughs: down from 400 µg/ft². EPA says these are the lowest levels that can be reliably and quickly measured in laboratories, and reflect standards New York City adopted in 2021. EPA now recommends abatement when dust-lead loadings are at or above these action levels.
• Below action levels: when dust-lead is at or above reportable levels but below action levels, EPA recommends best practices such as a HEPA-filter vacuum on furniture and other items, and regularly cleaning hard surfaces with a damp cloth or sponge and a general all-purpose cleaner.
• Test, don't guess: EPA's Protect Your Family booklet says the only way to find out if paint, dust or soil lead hazards exist is to test for them.

SOURCES
EPA – Hazard Standards and Clearance Levels for Lead in Paint, Dust and Soil: https://www.epa.gov/lead/hazard-standards-and-clearance-levels-lead-paint-dust-and-soil-tsca-sections-402-and-403

videos.title: Asbestos in an Older Home? Where EPA Says It May Hide, Room by Room #Shorts
videos.description:
Live in an older home? Asbestos was once common in building products. Here's where EPA says it may turn up, room by room — and the main rule.

KEY POINTS
• The main rule: EPA says asbestos-containing material in good condition that won't be disturbed (by remodeling, for example) is best left alone. Materials may release fibers when they are disturbed, damaged, removed improperly, repaired, cut, torn, sanded, sawed, drilled or scraped.
• Basement: EPA lists steam pipes, boilers and furnace ducts insulated with an asbestos blanket or asbestos paper tape among products that might have contained asbestos in the past.
• Kitchen and bath floors: resilient floor tiles (vinyl asbestos, asphalt and rubber), the backing on vinyl sheet flooring, and adhesives used for floor tile. EPA warns sanding tiles can release fibers and advises not to power grind or sand flooring, adhesive or backing.
• Ceilings and walls: some sprayed-on or troweled-on surface material may contain asbestos. EPA says firmly attached, hard, undamaged material should not be hazardous; if it produces powder or dust by hand pressure, seek professional advice.
• Around the wood stove: cement sheet, millboard and paper used as insulation around furnaces and wood-burning stoves.
• Planning a remodel: EPA says if in doubt, treat the material as if it contains asbestos and leave it alone; sealing, covering, repair or removal should be done by a professional trained to handle asbestos safely.
Note: you can't tell asbestos by looking — only lab analysis of a sample can confirm it.

videos.title: Do Cleaning Sprays Affect Your Lungs? A 20-Year Study of 6,235 Adults, Broken Down #Shorts
videos.description:
Could years of household cleaning sprays affect your lungs? A large European study followed adults for two decades. Here's what it found — and what it didn't.

KEY POINTS
• The study: Svanes et al. (2018, American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine) analyzed 6,235 participants from 22 centers in the European Community Respiratory Health Survey, measured at three time points over 20 years.
• What they measured: decline in lung function — FEV1 (air forcefully exhaled in one second) and FVC.
• The finding: compared with women not engaged in cleaning, FEV1 declined faster in women responsible for cleaning at home and in occupational cleaners. An accompanying editorial reports this as an extra 3.6 ml/yr (home) and 3.9 ml/yr (occupational) for FEV1.
• Sprays and more: both cleaning sprays and other cleaning agents were associated with accelerated FEV1 decline.
• What it didn't find: cleaning was not significantly associated with lung function decline in men, or with airway obstruction.
• How to read it: this is an observational cohort — an association, not proof of cause. The authors conclude cleaning exposures "may constitute a risk to long-term respiratory health."
• A cautious step: EPA lists cleansers and disinfectants among household VOC sources and advises increasing ventilation when using products that emit VOCs, using products according to manufacturer's directions, meeting or exceeding label precautions, and never mixing household care products unless the label directs.

SOURCES
Svanes et al. 2018, AJRCCM (PubMed): https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29451393/

videos.description:
Raking season in Wisconsin means some neighbors still burn leaves. Here's what state agencies say about that smoke, and how to keep it out of your house.

• Skip the burn pile: DNR's alternatives include mowing leaves into the lawn, composting, and municipal collection or drop-off. State law allows small amounts of dry leaves to be burned where local ordinances permit, but DNR discourages it because of air pollution.

videos.title: Washing Sheets for Dust Mites? 4 Laundry Myths vs NIH Research and Allergy Experts #Shorts
videos.description:
Washing sheets to fight dust mites? Four laundry myths, checked against NIH guidelines, peer-reviewed reviews and allergy experts.

KEY POINTS
• Myth 1 – Monthly is fine: the AAAAI says bedding should be washed weekly in hot water (130°F) and dried in a hot dryer; the NIH (NHLBI) asthma guidelines recommend washing the sheets and blankets on the bed weekly in hot water.
• Myth 2 – Cold does nothing: a peer-reviewed review notes hot water (over 130°F) killed all mites, while cold water reduced mite concentrations by 90%. videos.title: New Carpet Coming? EPA's 6-Point Air Checklist (Including the 72-Hour Rule) #Shorts
videos.description:
Getting new carpet before the holidays? New carpet, padding and adhesives give off VOCs for a while. Here's EPA's six-point checklist.

KEY POINTS
• Why: EPA says new carpet can be a source of chemical emissions — carpet emits volatile organic compounds, as do products that accompany installation such as adhesives and padding.
• 1 – Ask about emissions: ask the retailer for information to help select lower-emitting carpet, cushion and adhesives (EPA).
• 2 – Air it out first: ask the retailer to unroll and air out the carpet in a clean, well-ventilated area before installation.
• 3 – Plan to be out: consider leaving the premises during and immediately after installation, or schedule it when the space is unoccupied.
• 4 – Open up and exhaust: open doors and windows; during and after installation, use window fans and room air conditioners to exhaust fumes to the outdoors.
• 5 – Ventilate 72 hours: EPA's remodeling guidance says the typical recommendation is maximum ventilation during installation and for at least 72 hours after. EPA notes new carpet emissions can be significantly reduced, although not completely eliminated, in the first 72 hours with proper ventilation.
• 6 – Odor lingering: contact your carpet retailer if objectionable odors persist, and follow the manufacturer's instructions for carpet maintenance.
• Honest note: EPA says scientists have not been able to determine whether the chemicals emitted by new carpets are responsible for symptoms some consumers report.

videos.title: Stomach Bug at Home? CDC's 6-Step Norovirus Cleanup (Bleach Ratio + Laundry) #Shorts
videos.description:
When a stomach bug hits your household, cleanup matters. CDC notes norovirus can spread through tiny drops of vomit in the air. Here's its cleanup routine, step by step.

KEY POINTS
• Why it matters: CDC says tiny drops of vomit from an infected person can spray through the air and land on food or surfaces, and the CDC Yellow Book notes norovirus also spreads through contaminated surfaces and aerosols of vomit.
• Step 1 – Gloves on: protect yourself with disposable gloves, and a mask if you have one (CDC).
• Step 2 – Wipe and bag: wipe the entire area with paper towels and throw them in a plastic trash bag.
• Step 3 – Bleach, 5 minutes: CDC suggests a chlorine bleach solution of 1,000–5,000 ppm (5 to 25 tablespoons of household bleach [5%–8%] per gallon of water), or an EPA-registered disinfectant effective against norovirus. • Step 4 – Clean again: clean the entire area again with soap and hot water.
• Step 5 – Laundry, no shaking: immediately remove soiled clothes or linens, handle them carefully without shaking, wash with detergent and hot water at the maximum cycle length, then machine dry on the highest heat setting.
• Step 6 – Trash and hands: remove and toss gloves, take out the trash, and wash your hands with soap and water.

videos.title: Wet Carpet After a Leak? 3 Drying Mistakes to Avoid in the First 48 Hours (EPA) #Shorts
videos.description:
A burst hose or overflowing tub soaked the carpet? The first day or two matter most. Three drying mistakes to avoid, per EPA guidance.

KEY POINTS
• The 24–48 hour clock: EPA says that when water leaks or spills occur indoors, if wet or damp materials are dried within 24–48 hours, in most cases mold will not grow. (EPA notes this is a guideline — mold won't always grow after 48 hours, and may sometimes grow sooner.)
• Mistake 1 – Drying only the top: EPA's water-damage table lists carpet and backing — dry within 24–48 hours, and notes the subfloor under the carpet must also be cleaned and dried. Its mold course adds that carpet backing or padding must be dried in addition to the carpet, or mold will likely result.
• Lift it, don't just vacuum: EPA's mold course says wet vacuums alone will not dry carpets; wet carpets must be pulled up and dried, with fans blowing air over carpet and pad, then reinstalled.
• Mistake 2 – Fans on dirty water: EPA's drying guidelines are for clean water damage. Do not use fans before determining that the water is clean or sanitary. If water is contaminated with sewage or chemical or biological pollutants, OSHA requires protective equipment and containment, and an experienced professional should be consulted.
• Mistake 3 – Waiting it out: remove water with a water extraction (wet) vacuum while materials are still wet, reduce humidity with a dehumidifier, and accelerate drying with fans. If mold has already started to grow, EPA advises not using fans, since they may spread it.
• Fix the leak, too: if you clean up but don't fix the water problem, the mold problem will most likely come back (EPA).

SOURCES

videos.title: How to Swap a Furnace Filter the Right Way: 6 Steps From EPA and ENERGY STAR #Shorts
videos.description:
Heating season keeps your furnace filter busy. Here's how to swap it properly, in six steps from EPA and ENERGY STAR.

KEY POINTS
• Step 1 – Find the slot: depending on your system, your filter may be located in the duct system or in the heating and cooling equipment itself (ENERGY STAR). EPA notes furnace filters are installed either at the base of the air-handling unit or upstream in return grilles. Your contractor can show you how to change it.
• Step 2 – Power off first: EPA advises turning the power off while servicing central HVAC systems, and making an effort during filter replacement so pollutants are not re-emitted into the air and do not contact skin.
• Step 3 – Snug, not crushed: make sure the filter fits snugly so air does not leak around it, and you do not have to bend or crush the filter to make it fit (EPA). Bypass airflow significantly decreases filter effectiveness.
• Step 4 – Arrow with the airflow: EPA says filters should be installed so the directional arrow printed on the side points in the direction of airflow within the system.
• Step 5 – Pick the rating: use the highest-rated filter your system fan and filter slot can accommodate — ideally at least MERV 13 — and consult an HVAC technician to confirm what works for your system (EPA).
• Step 6 – Set a reminder: ENERGY STAR says check your filter every month, especially in heavy-use months; if it looks dirty, change it, and at a minimum change it every 3 months. EPA adds: follow the manufacturer's recommendations (typically every 60–90 days).

SOURCES

videos.title: Which Cooking Method Pollutes Your Kitchen Air Least? A 5-Method Study, Broken Down #Shorts
videos.description:
Which way of cooking puts the least pollution into your kitchen air? A peer-reviewed study tested five methods. Here's the breakdown — and its limits.

KEY POINTS
• The setup: University of Birmingham researchers prepared chicken breast with five methods — pan-frying, stir-frying, deep-frying, boiling and air-frying — in a well-controlled research kitchen, measuring particulate matter (PM) and volatile organic compounds (VOCs) with reference instruments (Tang et al., Indoor Air, 2024).
• Pan-frying peaked highest: median peak PM2.5 concentrations were pan-frying 92.9, stir-frying 26.7, deep-frying 7.7, boiling 0.7 and air-frying 0.6 micrograms per cubic meter.
• Air-frying near background: the lead author said PM levels from air-frying were so low they were hard to distinguish from background air.
• VOCs followed suit: median peak VOCs were pan-frying 260, deep-frying 230, stir-frying 110, boiling 30 and air-frying 20 parts per billion.
• It lingered: although cooking took about 10 minutes, the team recorded substantially higher pollutant levels in the kitchen for well over an hour afterward.
• Honest limits: one food (chicken breast) in one research kitchen. The authors found cooking temperature was the key factor linked to PM and VOC emission strength, and oil amount also influenced PM levels. A separate chamber study from the same group found air-fryer emissions vary by food, with high-fat foods producing more ultrafine particles.
• What helps: the researchers say opening windows or using extractor fans helps disperse pollutants, and continuing to ventilate after cooking helps avoid build-up.

SOURCES
Tang et al. (2024), Impact of Cooking Methods on Indoor Air Quality, Indoor Air (peer-reviewed): https://research.birmingham.ac.uk/en/publications/impact-of-cooking-methods-on-indoor-air-quality-a-comparative-stu/

videos.description:

• Guest room – think twice before closing it: a 2003 Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory study (Walker, LBNL-54005) found register closing led to increased energy use for typical California houses with ducts outside conditioned space, because savings were offset by increased duct losses, mostly duct leakage. • The 60% line: closing more than 60% of registers is not recommended, because the added flow resistance can lead furnaces to operate on the high-limit switch and cooling systems to suffer frozen coils (LBNL).
• If you must close one: the energy penalty was smallest when registers farthest from the air handler were closed first, since that mostly affects pressures in the closed-off branch (LBNL).
• Basement + attic ducts: DOE notes unsealed ducts in attics and crawlspaces lose air and uninsulated ducts lose heat.

videos.title: Mold, Damp Homes and Health: What the National Academies Could and Couldn't Prove #Shorts
videos.description:
In 2004, the Institute of Medicine (National Academies) reviewed the science on damp, moldy buildings and health. Here's what it found — and what it couldn't prove.

KEY POINTS
• Sufficient evidence of an association: damp indoor environments and some upper respiratory tract (nose and throat) symptoms, cough, wheeze, and asthma symptoms in sensitized persons. Indoor mold was also associated with hypersensitivity pneumonitis in susceptible persons (IOM 2004).
• Association is not causation: the committee concluded no outcome met its category of "sufficient evidence of a causal relationship" (IOM 2004).
• Limited or suggestive evidence: shortness of breath (dyspnea), lower respiratory illness in otherwise-healthy children, and the development of asthma in susceptible persons (IOM 2004).
• Fatigue, neuropsychiatric disorders and other health problems attributed to moldy buildings: very few studies; the little evidence available did not support an association, but the committee could not rule out the possibility (National Academies).
• Since then: a 2011 review in Environmental Health Perspectives (Mendell et al.) found sufficient evidence of association for additional outcomes, including asthma development, while agreeing that causation was not established for most outcomes.
• Universal agreement: promptly fixing leaks and cleaning up spills or standing water substantially reduces the potential for mold growth (National Academies).
• Bottom line: the evidence on indoor mold toxins (mycotoxins) and wider illness remains limited. Fix moisture and remove mold rather than guessing.

videos.title: Box Fan + Furnace Filter: What EPA's DIY Air Cleaner Lab Tests Found #Shorts
videos.description:
Can a box fan and a furnace filter really clean smoky air? EPA scientists tested do-it-yourself air cleaners in the lab. Here's what they found.

KEY POINTS
• Setup: EPA researchers used simulated wildfire smoke (smoldering pine needles) in a room-sized chamber to measure the clean air delivery rate (CADR) of DIY air cleaner designs (Holder et al., 2022, Indoor Air).
• Basic design — box fan with one 1-inch MERV 13 filter: wildfire smoke CADR ≈ 111.
• Adding a no-cost cardboard shroud: ≈ 156. One 4-inch MERV 13 + shroud: ≈ 248. Two 1-inch filters + shroud: ≈ 263. Corsi-Rosenthal box (four 1-inch MERV 13 filters + shroud): ≈ 401.
• DIY air cleaners with dirty filters loaded with smoke or dust were almost completely ineffective — keep extra filters and replace them when dirty (EPA).
• Safety: use a newer box fan (2012 or newer) with a UL or ETL mark; align the filter's airflow arrows with the fan's airflow and make a good seal (EPA).

KEY POINTS

videos.title: MERV Ratings Decoded: What 11, 13 and HEPA Really Catch #Shorts
videos.description:
That number on your furnace filter has a specific meaning. Here's how MERV works, by the numbers.

KEY POINTS
• MERV (Minimum Efficiency Reporting Value) runs from 1 to 16 and reports a filter's ability to capture particles between 0.3 and 10 microns (ASHRAE Standard 52.2).
• The smallest tested range, 0.3–1 µm, makes up a significant fraction of PM2.5 — but filters are only explicitly tested on it at MERV 11 and above.
• MERV 11: at least 20% removal of 0.3–1 µm particles.
• MERV 13: at least 50% for 0.3–1 µm, at least 85% for 1–3 µm, and at least 90% for 3–10 µm.
• HEPA is rated separately (not on the MERV scale) and can theoretically remove at least 99.97% of 0.3-µm particles; true HEPA filters usually aren't installed in residential HVAC and would likely require professional modification.
• EPA: choose at least MERV 13, or as high as your system fan and filter slot can accommodate; consult an HVAC technician if unsure, and follow the manufacturer's replacement schedule.

videos.title: Do Houseplants Clean Indoor Air? What 30 Years of Studies Show #Shorts
videos.description:
Can a few houseplants purify the air at home? A review of 30 years of chamber studies did the math.

KEY POINTS
• Classic "plants clean air" results came from small sealed chambers (often 1 m³ or less) where a single VOC was injected and tracked for hours or days.
• Cummings & Waring (J Expo Sci Environ Epidemiol, 2020) reviewed 12 published studies and translated 196 results into clean air delivery rate (CADR), the standard air-cleaner metric.
• Median single-plant CADR was about 0.023 m³/h — meaning 10–1,000 plants per square meter of floor space would be needed to match the VOC removal that normal outdoor-air exchange already provides.
• The American Lung Association translates that to roughly 680 plants in a 1,500 sq ft home.
• Caveat: real-home studies are few, and most did not measure ventilation, so isolating any small plant effect is difficult. Plants may still have well-being benefits.
• EPA: source control is usually the most effective way to improve indoor air; increasing outdoor air is another approach.

Three numbers decide whether your winter air is too dry, just right, or feeding dust mites and window sweat.
